questions.stem: An application executes $6.4 \times 10^8$ number of instructions in $6.3$ seconds. There are four types of instructions, the details of which are given in the table. The duration of a clock cycle in nanoseconds is _________. (rounded off to one decimal place)

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: A clock cycle is one tick of the processor clock, and its duration is the clock period. CPI (cycles per instruction) says how many ticks one instruction of a given type needs. A processor that runs without overlap spends, for each type, (number of instructions) times (CPI) ticks. The one rule: total execution time = total clock cycles times clock period, so the period is the time divided by the total number of cycles.

steps.title: Count cycles for each instruction type
steps.body: Multiply each count by its CPI. Branch: $2.25\times10^8 \times 2 = 4.5\times10^8$. Load: $1.20\times10^8 \times 5 = 6.0\times10^8$. Store: $1.65\times10^8 \times 4 = 6.6\times10^8$. Arithmetic: $1.30\times10^8 \times 3 = 3.9\times10^8$.

steps.title: Add and divide
steps.body: Total cycles $= (4.5+6.0+6.6+3.9)\times10^8 = 21\times10^8 = 2.1\times10^9$. The period is $6.3 \text{ s} / 2.1\times10^9 = 3\times10^{-9}$ s, which is 3.0 ns. The instruction total ($6.4\times10^8$) is only a consistency check; the table counts sum to $6.4\times10^8$ as well.

shortcut.body: Work in units of $10^8$: cycles are $4.5+6+6.6+3.9 = 21$, so $2.1\times10^9$ cycles; $6.3/2.1 = 3$, and $10^{-9}$ s is 1 ns. About one minute.

traps.text: Using the instruction count $6.4\times10^8$ instead of the cycle count gives $6.3/6.4\times10^8 \approx 9.8$ ns. Time per instruction is not time per cycle.
Averaging the CPIs without weights, $(2+5+4+3)/4 = 3.5$, gives $2.24\times10^9$ cycles and 2.8 ns. CPI must be weighted by instruction counts.
Reporting the period in seconds or microseconds ($3\times10^{-9}$) instead of nanoseconds.

recognize.clues: The table gives a CPI and an instruction count for each type, plus a total run time, and asks for the clock period. That is the classic "time = cycles x period" setup for a processor that spends several cycles per instruction.
recognize.contrast: Do not use the average-CPI-per-instruction formula on the instruction total alone; that gives time per instruction. The period needs total cycles, which comes from the weighted sum of the table.

check.body: Rebuild the cycle total from instruction fractions instead of raw cycle counts. The mix is $225/640 = 0.3516$ branch, $120/640 = 0.1875$ load, $165/640 = 0.2578$ store and $130/640 = 0.2031$ arithmetic, so the weighted mean CPI is $0.3516\times2 + 0.1875\times5 + 0.2578\times4 + 0.2031\times3 \approx 3.281$. Times $6.4\times10^8$ instructions this is about $2.1\times10^9$ cycles, matching the sum above. Units: $2.1\times10^9$ cycles $\times\ 3$ ns $= 6.3$ s, the stated run time.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 question 51
GATE 2025 CS-2 final answer key, IIT Roorkee

hints.text: The question wants a time per clock tick, but you are given a time for the whole run. What must you know about the run before you can split that time into ticks?
CPI says how many ticks one instruction of a type takes, so instructions and ticks are different counts. Which of the two does the clock period divide into?
Execution time equals total ticks times the length of one tick. Total ticks is found by weighting each type's CPI by how many instructions of that type ran.
Build one column of (count times CPI) for the four rows, add the column, then divide the given time by that sum. Keep the powers of ten in one unit to avoid slips.
The branch row alone contributes $2.25\times10^8 \times 2 = 4.5\times10^8$ ticks. Do the other three rows the same way before adding.

variation.stem: A program executes $5.6 \times 10^8$ instructions in $3.0$ seconds. The instruction mix is: type P with CPI 1 and $1.0\times10^8$ instructions, type Q with CPI 2 and $2.5\times10^8$ instructions, type R with CPI 4 and $1.5\times10^8$ instructions, type S with CPI 5 and $0.6\times10^8$ instructions. The clock period in nanoseconds is _________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
variation.explanation: Cycles are $1.0\times1 + 2.5\times2 + 1.5\times4 + 0.6\times5 = 15$ in units of $10^8$, so $1.5\times10^9$ cycles. The period is $3.0 / 1.5\times10^9 = 2.0\times10^{-9}$ s, which is 2.0 ns. Dividing by the instruction count would give about 5.4 ns, and an unweighted CPI average of 3 would give about 1.8 ns.

questions.stem: A partial data path of a processor is given in the figure, where RA, RB, and RZ are 32-bit registers. Which option(s) is/are CORRECT related to arithmetic operations using the data path as shown?
questions.figure: RA (32 bit) feeds one input of Mux_A, and a 32-bit immediate value feeds the other input of Mux_A; a control line "Select RA/immediate" chooses between them. RB (32 bit) feeds Mux_B in the same way, with its own 32-bit immediate input and a control line "Select RB/immediate". The outputs of Mux_A and Mux_B are the two 32-bit inputs of the ALU. The ALU has "ALU control" lines and its 32-bit output goes to register RZ (32 bit).
options: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two registers.
The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.
The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two immediate values.
The data path can only implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.

diagram.alt: Data path: RA and an immediate value feed Mux_A, RB and an immediate value feed Mux_B, both muxes feed the ALU, and the ALU writes RZ.

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of the four select settings of the two multiplexers and the operand pair each gives the ALU.

steps.title: Define the parts and the rule
steps.body: A multiplexer (mux) is a switch with several data inputs and one output; a select line decides which input is passed on. An immediate value is a constant stored inside the instruction itself. The ALU (arithmetic logic unit) combines its two inputs as the control lines say. The rule: whatever the two muxes can deliver, in every combination, is what the ALU can be given, because each mux has its own independent select line.

steps.title: Read the figure
steps.body: Mux_A chooses between RA and an immediate. Mux_B chooses between RB and an immediate. The two select lines are separate, so each mux is set without regard to the other. The ALU receives one output from each mux.

steps.title: List the four combinations
steps.body: (RA, RB): two registers. (RA, immediate): one register and one immediate. (immediate, RB): one immediate and one register. (immediate, immediate): two immediates. All four are possible, so the ALU can add, subtract and so on in each case.

steps.title: Judge each option
steps.body: (A) true: select RA and RB. (B) true: select RA with the immediate on Mux_B, or the immediate on Mux_A with RB. (C) true: select the immediate on both muxes. (D) false: it claims register plus immediate is the only possibility, but rows 1 and 4 of the list contradict it. Answer: A, B, C.

shortcut.body: Two independent 2-to-1 muxes give $2\times2=4$ operand pairs, and the figure shows no restriction. Any option that says "only" is almost certainly false. Ten seconds. It is unsafe only if a figure ties both selects to one line; here there are two separate lines.

traps.text: Option D: thinking an immediate must always be paired with a register, as in an add-immediate instruction. The hardware allows more; which pairs an instruction set uses is a separate matter.
Option C: leaving it out because no real instruction adds two constants. The question asks what the data path can do, and both muxes can select an immediate.
Option A and B are the true statements candidates skip when they think only "which is the one typical case". In an MSQ every true statement must be chosen, and there is no partial credit.

recognize.clues: The figure shows two multiplexers, each with its own select line, feeding the two ALU inputs, with registers and an immediate as sources. Statements about which operand pairs are possible are answered by tracing paths through those multiplexers.
recognize.contrast: This is a data-path capability question, not an instruction-set question. Which operand forms a real instruction set offers is a separate matter from what the wiring permits.

check.body: Test the extreme settings directly. Set both selects to the register side and the ALU sees RA and RB. Set both to the immediate side and it sees two immediates. Because the two switches move independently, the mixed settings follow. A single option claiming only one pairing is contradicted by the first two settings.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 question 17
GATE 2025 CS-1 final answer key, IIT Roorkee

hints.text: The question is about what the hardware allows, not about which instructions a real program would use. What decides the pair of values the ALU receives?
A multiplexer passes exactly one of its inputs, chosen by its select line. Each of the two multiplexers here feeds one ALU input.
When two selectors are controlled by separate lines, every choice on one side can be paired with every choice on the other. Count the pairs, then test each option against that list.

Write the two choices at the first multiplexer and the two at the second, then list all pairings. For each option, ask whether its pair of operand kinds appears in your list, and whether the word "only" is justified.

variation.stem: In a data path, Mux_A selects between RA and a 32-bit immediate and feeds the left ALU input. RB is wired directly to the right ALU input with no multiplexer. The ALU output goes to RZ. Which option(s) is/are CORRECT about the arithmetic operations this data path can perform?
options: It can operate on RA and RB.
It can operate on an immediate value (left) and RB.
It can operate on two immediate values.
It can operate on RA and an immediate value placed on the right input.
variation.explanation: Only the left input has a choice, so the possible pairs are (RA, RB) and (immediate, RB). Options A and B are therefore true. The right input always carries RB, so two immediates and RA with an immediate on the right are both impossible.

questions.stem:
Consider the following data path diagram.

Consider an instruction: R0 $\leftarrow$ R1 + R2. The following steps are used to execute it over the given data path. Assume that PC is incremented appropriately. The subscripts r and w indicate read and write operations, respectively.

1. R2$_r$, TEMP1$_r$, ALU$_{add}$, TEMP2$_w$
2. R1$_r$, TEMP1$_w$
3. PC$_r$, MAR$_w$, MEM$_r$
4. TEMP2$_r$, R0$_w$
5. MDR$_r$, IR$_w$

Which one of the following is the correct order of execution of the above steps?
questions.figure: A single BUS runs across the top. Connected to the bus are MAR, MDR, IR, PC and the register file R0, R1, ..., R7. MAR and MDR each have a link marked "To Memory". The register file, TEMP2 and TEMP1 are also on the bus. The bus feeds the left input of the ALU and TEMP1 feeds the right input. The ALU output goes to TEMP2, and TEMP2 connects back to the bus.

diagram.alt: Single-bus data path with MAR, MDR, IR, PC, registers R0 to R7, TEMP1, TEMP2 and the ALU.

solutionDiagram.alt: Five rows in time order: step 3, 5, 2, 1, 4, labelled fetch, execute and write back.

steps.title: Define the terms and the rule
steps.body: A data path is the set of registers, buses and the ALU that instructions move data through. This one has a single bus, so only one value can travel on it at a time; that is why temporary registers TEMP1 and TEMP2 exist. A micro-step such as R1$_r$ means "put R1 on the bus" and TEMP1$_w$ means "latch the bus into TEMP1". The rule that decides the question: a register can only be read after something has written it, and an instruction can only execute after it has been fetched into IR.

steps.title: Fetch comes first
steps.body: Step 3 puts PC on the bus, latches it into MAR and starts the memory read. Step 5 then takes the word memory returned in MDR and latches it into IR. So 3 precedes 5, and both precede the execution steps, since the instruction must be in IR before it can be carried out.

steps.title: Order the execution steps by data dependence
steps.body: Step 1 reads TEMP1 as an ALU input, so TEMP1 must already hold R1: step 2 (R1$_r$, TEMP1$_w$) must come first. Step 1 puts R2 on the bus as the other ALU input and writes the sum into TEMP2. Step 4 reads TEMP2 into R0, so it must come after step 1. The execution order is 2, 1, 4.

steps.title: Combine and match
steps.body: Fetch 3, 5, then execute 2, 1, 4 gives 3, 5, 2, 1, 4. This is option C. A script checking all four options against these three dependencies leaves only C.

shortcut.body: Fetch always starts an instruction, so the first two must be 3 then 5: that keeps C and D. Between them, 1 reads TEMP1, so the step writing TEMP1 (step 2) must precede it, which rules out D. About one minute.

traps.text: Option A starts with execution steps and puts the fetch at the end, as if the instruction could run before it is in IR.
Option B reads TEMP1 in step 1 before step 2 loads it, and fetches last. Both break the rule that a register must be written before it is read.
Option D has the right fetch but runs step 1 before step 2, so the ALU adds with a TEMP1 that does not yet hold R1.

recognize.clues: The stem lists numbered micro-steps with read and write subscripts on a single-bus data path and asks for their order, so the task is sequencing control steps by data dependence, with the instruction fetch at the start.
recognize.contrast: This is not a pipeline hazard question. There is one instruction and one bus, so the order is forced by fetch-then-execute and by write-before-read on TEMP1 and TEMP2, not by overlap.

check.body: Replay the order on the data path and track what each register holds. After the fetch steps IR holds the instruction. The next step puts R1 into TEMP1, the one after that adds TEMP1 and R2 into TEMP2, and the last copies TEMP2 into R0. Every read finds a value already written. Swapping any adjacent pair of the execution steps would read a stale TEMP1 or TEMP2.

sources.label: GATE 2020 CS answer key, IIT Delhi

hints.text: Which of the five steps can run when the instruction is not yet known? Start by asking what has to happen before any step of R0 = R1 + R2 can be carried out.
On a single-bus data path, an instruction is first read from memory into IR using the PC and MAR. Only then do the register-transfer steps for the instruction itself run.
A value can be read from a register only after something has written it. Follow each register or temporary named in the steps and see which step writes it and which step reads it.
Split the steps into fetch steps and execution steps. Among the execution steps, draw an arrow from the step that writes TEMP1 to the one that reads it, and the same for TEMP2.
The step that writes TEMP2 is the one that also performs the addition. The step that copies a result into R0 must therefore come after it.

variation.stem: On the same single-bus data path, consider R3 <- R4 - R5. The steps are: 1. R5$_r$, TEMP1$_w$; 2. TEMP2$_r$, R3$_w$; 3. PC$_r$, MAR$_w$, MEM$_r$; 4. R4$_r$, TEMP1$_r$, ALU$_{sub}$, TEMP2$_w$; 5. MDR$_r$, IR$_w$. Which one is the correct order of execution?
variation.explanation: Fetch comes first: step 3 loads MAR and starts the memory read, then step 5 moves the word into IR. Of the execution steps, step 1 must write TEMP1 before step 4 reads it, and step 2 must read TEMP2 only after step 4 writes it, giving 1, 4, 2. Option B reads TEMP1 before it is loaded, C executes before the fetch, and D latches IR before the memory read has started.
